quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen at natural speed: does "praise your" keep two distinct consonant sounds at the boundary, or blend them into a new one?
quests.explanation: In relaxed, natural speech, /z/ and /j/ rarely stay separate at a word boundary like this one. They coalesce into /ʒ/, exactly as in "praise your".
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The 'r' in "answer" isn't always pronounced. Does the vowel at the start of "it" bring it back to life?
quests.explanation: Because the letter 'r' genuinely exists at the end of "answer", its reappearance before the vowel in "it" is called linking /r/ — a real, spelled sound resurfacing, unlike intrusive /r/, which comes from nowhere in the spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "for" isn't the stressed word in "ask for help". What usually happens to an unstressed function word's vowel in fast speech?
quests.explanation: This is a weak form: "for" keeps its full vowel /ɔː/ only when stressed or said alone. In natural speech like "ask for help", it reduces to schwa because it carries no sentence stress.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try stressing every word in "fish and chips" equally — it sounds stiff and unnatural, right? Which word loses its full vowel to fix that?
quests.explanation: English sentence rhythm relies on this kind of reduction — content words stay strong, function words like "and" go weak. That's why /æ/ becomes schwa in "fish and chips".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two vowels back to back is awkward to say smoothly. What sound does natural speech add between "new" and "arrival" — despite it not appearing in either word's spelling?
quests.explanation: This is a purely phonetic addition: /w/ shows up between "new" and "arrival" only to ease pronunciation, with nothing in either word's spelling to account for it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /t/ at the end of "almost". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "ready"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /t/ at the end of "almost" disappears before the consonant that starts "ready".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "bulb"'s bilabial sound before it even finishes "light". What happens to /t/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /t/ to /p/ at the end of "light" happens because the following bilabial consonant in "bulb" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "ten" and "boxes" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /n/ ending "ten" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "boxes", surfacing as /m/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Function words like "but" rarely keep their dictionary pronunciation in natural sentences. Listen for what its vowel becomes in "wait, but I".
quests.explanation: Because "but" isn't emphasized in "wait, but I", its vowel weakens from the full /ʌ/ to a fast, neutral schwa sound. This happens to almost every unstressed function word in fluent English.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In "we must go", one word carries no stress at all. Focus on "must" — what happens to its vowel as a result?
quests.explanation: Weak forms like this one are what make native speech sound smooth rather than choppy. "must" trades its citation vowel /ʌ/ for schwa whenever it's unstressed, as it is in "we must go".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This 'r' is real — it's written into "mother" — but often silent. Listen for it specifically at the boundary with "and".
quests.explanation: Speakers keep the /r/ silent in "mother" only until a vowel gives it a reason to surface. "and" provides exactly that vowel, so the /r/ links the phrase together.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say the phrase at normal speed. Does the final consonant of "warm" stay cleanly inside "warm", or does it glide forward into "up"?
quests.explanation: This kind of linking happens constantly in natural English: a final consonant reaches across the word boundary to join the next vowel, connecting "warm" and "up" into one flowing phrase.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "send" and the /j/ starting "yourself" don't survive as separate sounds in fast speech. What do they turn into together?
quests.explanation: This is why "send yourself" doesn't sound like two crisp, separate words: the boundary consonant /d/ and the /j/ of "yourself" merge into the single sound /dʒ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "they have gone" quickly, the way you would in real conversation. Does "have" sound the same as when you say it alone?
quests.explanation: Say "have" on its own and you get the full vowel /æ/. Say it inside "they have gone" at natural speed, and it reduces to schwa — the standard weak form.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "are" said by itself has a full, clear vowel. Said inside "what time are we" at natural speed, does that vowel survive?
quests.explanation: This reduction isn't sloppy speech — it's a predictable, rule-governed feature of English. Unstressed "are" reduces from /ɑː/ to schwa in virtually every natural sentence, including "what time are we".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Content words — nouns, verbs, adjectives — usually keep their full vowels; function words like "can" often don't. What happens to it in "can you hear me"?
quests.explanation: Stress timing in English means unstressed words get compressed. "can" loses its full /æ/ vowel and reduces to schwa here, keeping "can you hear me" flowing at a natural rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the schwa. Somewhere in "cup of tea", a full vowel gets flattened into that quick, neutral "uh" sound — which word is it?
quests.explanation: Native listeners expect this weak form; a fully stressed /ɒ/ on "of" in "cup of tea" would actually sound unnatural or overly formal. The relaxed schwa is the normal, expected pronunciation.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "some" is grammatically necessary but rarely emphasized. What does that lack of stress do to its vowel in "save some money"?
quests.explanation: This is one of the most common patterns in spoken English: function words reduce, content words don't. "some" follows that rule exactly, shrinking from /ʌ/ to schwa in "save some money".
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Unlike a sound added from nowhere, the /r/ here is already part of "partner"'s spelling. What triggers it to reappear before "and"?
quests.explanation: This linking /r/ is predictable from spelling alone: any r-final word behaves this way before a vowel, and "partner and" is a clean example of it.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "ten" — it's still there, just different. What does /n/ turn into before the velar sound in "countries"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /n/ ending "ten" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /ŋ/ to match the velar sound beginning "countries".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "he was late" at a natural conversational pace. Does "was" keep its full vowel sound, or shrink to a quick "uh"?
quests.explanation: Unstressed function words like "was" almost always reduce their vowel to schwa /ə/ in connected speech. Its full form is /ɒ/, but in "he was late" it shrinks to something much quicker and quieter.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Nothing in "extra"'s ending suggests a consonant at all. So the /r/ you might hear before "information" isn't really part of either word — where does it come from?
quests.explanation: Vowel hiatus (two vowels in a row) is uncomfortable in fluent English, so an intrusive /r/ fills the gap in "extra information" — a sound created by the flow of speech, not by spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "for" isn't the stressed word in "waiting for the bus". What usually happens to an unstressed function word's vowel in fast speech?
quests.explanation: This is a weak form: "for" keeps its full vowel /ɔː/ only when stressed or said alone. In natural speech like "waiting for the bus", it reduces to schwa because it carries no sentence stress.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "grand finale" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /d/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "grand finale", the /d/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ at the end of "net" is about to meet a velar sound in "cost". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a velar consonant, /t/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "net cost", /t/ becomes /k/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "soft" meets "drink" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "soft drink" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "Asia" has no letter for /r/ anywhere at its end. So if you hear a /r/ before "and", where does it actually come from?
quests.explanation: English avoids putting two vowel sounds directly next to each other, so speakers insert a small linking sound to bridge them. Since "Asia" has no /r/ in its spelling, this /r/ is intrusive — added purely for smoothness, not because it's really part of "Asia" or "and".
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Both "schema" and "of" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "schema of", an intrusive /r/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a sound-merging boundary. What new consonant replaces /s/ + /j/ when you say "this yard" naturally?
quests.explanation: Coalescence is a genuine sound change, not just fast talking — /s/ plus /j/ reliably becomes /ʃ/ in phrases like "this yard" across natural English speech.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "see other" without a pause. Two vowel sounds are about to collide — what does English insert to smooth the transition?
quests.explanation: Because "see" ends in a vowel and "other" begins with one, English speakers instinctively insert /j/ between them. It's not in the spelling of either word — it's added on the fly to keep the speech flowing.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.
